How do forecasting models compete, qualify and serve daily natural gas predictions in production? The page presents my natural-gas-forecasting project as a forecast in production: what production forecasts today and which model serves each horizon first, then the tournament standings behind it and the backtests every score starts from. Every model is measured with the same four numbers: MAE, MAPE, WAPE and bias. The forecast target is the daily high of the front-month natural gas futures contract (Yahoo Finance NG=F), in dollars per MMBtu. Weather in major gas-demand cities and EIA weekly storage are the inputs. All of it is public data.

The forecasting repository runs a daily tournament. Each model family (Chronos-2, gradient boosting, Greykite) has a champion and a challenger in its own MLflow registry, and naive is the baseline. The champions compete in three horizon events: days 1 to 5, days 6 to 15 and days 16 to 30. A champion qualifies for an event when it beats naive there by at least 1% on blended MAE, which mixes its last 30 matured production days with its backtest MAE, and the lowest qualified score wins. When nobody qualifies, naive wins. The three winners are stitched into the production forecast. A challenger takes its family's title after 60 matured production days ahead of its champion.

Top of the page. What it shows: The question, data and approach, three key findings (how the tournament runs, which models serve production and the 30 day accuracy profile), and four cards for the best model over all 30 backtest days: MAE, MAPE, WAPE and bias, each next to naive.

Active predictions in production. What it shows: A scoring run dropdown, newest run first and selected by default. The chart shows the stitched production path for that run, colored by the model behind each segment. The family champions and the naive baseline can be added as dotted lines. The run details give the run id, as-of date, scoring time, horizon and contender count, and the forecast model card shows the model serving each segment, in its color, with its role and its backtest MAE, MAPE, WAPE and bias for that horizon.

Model leaderboard. What it shows: One card per event with the winning model, its role and blended MAE, and its MAPE, WAPE and bias for that horizon. Below them, a collapsible model scoreboard, closed by default. Opened, it shows the standings for the selected horizon (days 1 to 5, 6 to 15, 16 to 30 or all days): rank, model and role, blended MAE, backtest MAE, production MAE and weight, and a status (winner, qualified, below the 1% bar, in trials, baseline).

Model selection backtests. What it shows: The rolling-origin backtests used to train and tune each family, which seed every blended score. A slider over all 125 as-of dates shows the price history, the Chronos-2 forecast, a second model of your choice and the actuals, with each model's MAE for that date. Below it, MAE, MAPE, WAPE and bias per family by horizon.

section: Natural Gas Price Forecast > The snapshot
text: ForecastSnapshotBuilder opens data/natgas.db read only (mode=ro) and reads outputs/backtest_forecasts.parquet, checking its row count against the database table. It writes the backtest forecasts, settled prices, every prediction (the stitched production stage, each contender stage such as chronos:champion or baseline:naive, and the legacy:* rows from before the tournament), matured actuals, the two accuracy views and the tournament tables (tournament_standings, event_winners, challenger_trials, promotion_history) as parquet, plus metadata.json. A database from before the tournament gives empty tournament tables, and the page says so. A price bar loaded on its own trading day is left for the next refresh, since that session may still be trading. Run it again after each scoring run to pick up new predictions and actuals. Without the source folder it says so and leaves the current snapshot alone, and without a snapshot the page still renders with a short note. Nothing is scored or refit here.

The site runs on Render's Starter plan, described in render.yaml. The build installs the project, and gunicorn serves app:server on the port Render provides. Pages read only the committed caches in cache/ and cache/natgas/, so Headline Radar and the forecasting repository are not needed at runtime. Connect the GitHub repository to Render, then set CHATBOT_API_URL (and CHATBOT_API_KEY if the Ask service requires one) in the dashboard. Add ajgeiger.com as a custom domain and point its Cloudflare DNS records at the values Render shows. Render issues the certificate once the records are in place.

Headline Radar pulls live news headlines from GDELT and seven RSS feeds into a local database, then finds the topics in them with a topic model I wrote from scratch. Every 15 minutes there are thousands of new headlines. Headline Radar groups them into a few hundred readable topics, names each one with keywords, and shows how the topics relate. See the full walkthrough: Topic model notebook

See the full walkthrough: Topic model notebook How to read this chart: each row on the right is a topic, with its top keywords and its number of articles. Lines join topics that use similar words. The further left two branches meet, the less alike they are, so pairs that join close to the right are the most similar. In this run, the Ukraine and Russia topic sits next to the Gaza and Israel topic, and NFL joins college football (CFP, Notre Dame). The closest pair is crashes and injuries next to police, arrests, and charges. Stock market headlines sit beside Black Friday and iPhone deals. The chart covers 41,277 articles and 283 topics.

Most organizations have more free text than anyone can read. Topic modeling turns that text into a short list of themes you can count, track, and act on. Spot new stories and market-moving themes early, as a new topic appears or grows. Track how coverage of a company, sector, or region changes from week to week. Route and triage a large stream of headlines to the right people. The engine does not know anything about news. Point it at any column of short texts and it works the same way. Good fits are support tickets, customer feedback, invoice or claim notes, and survey responses.

I am a Lead Applied AI Scientist. At Signature Aviation I built the enterprise AI platform, covering data engineering, forecasting, dynamic pricing, and MLOps governance. This project shows the same habits on open data. My own BERTopic-style model, not a black box. Sentence embeddings with attention-mask mean pooling, UMAP to reduce them, HDBSCAN to cluster them, and c-TF-IDF to name the topics. Each step is a small, readable method. A loader you can rerun safely. Each article id is the SHA-256 of its URL, so reloads never add duplicates. A watermark per source means each run only pulls new data.

Clear handling of edge cases. Topic -1 means a text did not fit any topic. Topic -2 means the text was blank. The two are never mixed. Honest predictions. For each text, transform_with_status says whether it was in the training data (seen), was predicted (new), or was blank. Safe joins. TopicJoiner adds topic ids to a table without ever adding rows, and it raises an error when the data has drifted from the fitted model. Diagnostics you can check. get_fit_diagnostics shows how cluster sizes changed after identical texts were given one shared topic. The right size of tools. pandas and SQLite instead of Spark and a database server, because the data fits on one machine.

Tested on real data. 41,277 articles became 283 topics, with 40% left as outliers. The full run took about 3.5 minutes on CPU. Some topics pick up publisher boilerplate, such as "targeted news service". The example texts for each topic make those easy to spot and relabel.

models/TopicModel.py works on any list of short texts. Embed each unique text with TextEmbedder (MiniLM). Reduce the embeddings to 5 dimensions with UMAP. Give identical texts the same topic. Move any topic smaller than min_topic_size to the outliers. Number topics by size, so topic 0 is the largest. Describe each topic with c-TF-IDF keywords and three example texts. Texts from the fit data get their fitted topic back. New texts are placed with HDBSCAN approximate_predict. The model only knows the data it was fit on, so refit it as new headlines arrive.

TopicJoiner adds a topic_id column to a pandas DataFrame by exact text match. It never adds rows and gives blank text -2. It raises an error if one text has two topic ids, or if a text is missing from the lookup, which means the model needs a refit.

data/headline_radar.db is a SQLite file with three tables. The schema lives in utils/storage/Database.py. The tables are linked by the source name (gdelt or rss). These links are by value only. There are no foreign key constraints. No duplicates on reload. articles.id is the SHA-256 of the URL, and inserts use INSERT OR IGNORE, so rerunning a load skips articles that are already stored. Incremental loads. watermarks keeps one high-water mark per source. The next run starts from it and only pulls new data.

An audit log. load_runs gets one row per run, with its status, counts fetched, inserted, and skipped, the high-water mark it reached, and any error. Blanks stay blank. Missing titles or descriptions are stored as NULL, and the row is kept. Zero setup. SQLite needs no server. Timestamps are stored as UTC text and the SQL is plain, so moving to Postgres later is simple.

GDELT data comes from the 15-minute GKG files advertised by https://data.gdeltproject.org/gdeltv2/lastupdate.txt. Titles are read from the GKG PAGE_TITLE extras field; a precise publish time is used when PAGE_PRECISEPUBTIMESTAMP is present, otherwise the 15-minute file time. GKG does not include article descriptions, so those are stored as NULL. Files are downloaded over HTTPS; the HTTP URLs in lastupdate.txt often return 500. The very newest file listed in lastupdate can 404 for a short time and is retried on the next run. The GDELT DOC 2.0 API also exposes titles, but it rate-limits to one request every five seconds and, during setup, frequently returned HTTP 429 or an empty JSON object, so it is not used here.

RSS feeds included here: BBC News, NPR News, CNBC Top Stories, Guardian Business, MarketWatch, NYT World, and Al Jazeera. Feeds that did not respond during setup (Yahoo Finance 404, Politico 403, CNN SSL error) were left out.

Start here: grid search backtest notebook. It runs every model on the same 125 rolling as-of dates, forecasts 30 trading days ahead from each, scores them, and publishes the winner to the MLflow model registry. The Bayesian search notebook repeats the search with Optuna. Every day after that, the model tournament turns the results into one published forecast: each model family's champion competes in three horizon events, and the event winners make up the business facing forecast.

Natural gas is one of the most volatile commodities there is. Utilities, power plants, and industrial buyers plan purchases days and weeks ahead, and a few cents per MMBtu on millions of MMBtu is real money. Weather drives demand, storage shows how tight supply is, and the futures price reacts to both.

Most forecasting demos stop at one model on one train and test split. This project is built the way a production team would want it: every model is backtested on the same dates with no look-ahead, every run is logged, and a model only replaces the baseline when it earns it. In production that rule becomes a tournament: challengers prove themselves over 60 live days before they take a title, and each horizon of the published forecast goes to whichever champion is actually best at it.

Prices from 2015-01-02 to 2026-11-18. 125 as-of dates every 14 days from 2021-12-31 to 2026-10-02, each forecasting the next 30 trading days (backtest.horizon_days in config/tuning.yaml). The two as-of dates after 2026-10-02 are skipped because 30 trading days of actuals do not exist yet. Same dates for every model. Best config per model, MAE, RMSE, and bias in dollars per MMBtu, MAPE and WAPE in percent. Grid search (61 configs):

Chronos-2 beat naive by 1.28 percent in grid search, clearing the 1 percent margin, so the publisher registered it as natgas-price-forecaster version 8 (@champion), the same config as version 7. Bayesian search found Chronos-2 at context 320 without weather, only 0.74 percent better than naive, so on its own it would keep naive. What the numbers say: Over 5 days nothing beats repeating the last price. Over 30 days Chronos-2 pulls ahead, and the gap grows with the horizon: it trails naive on days 1 to 5 and leads on days 16 to 30.

Chronos-2 does not need weather to win. Without it, context 512 scores MAE 0.5204, 1.05 percent better than naive, with a lower RMSE (0.7774) than the weather config. Weather helps a little, but backtests hand it perfect weather for all 30 days, so treat that gain as an upper bound.

Yearly terms help gradient boosting a little and hurt Chronos-2. In the grid they lower gradient boosting MAE in 14 of 16 matched configs (0.0046 on average) and the best drops from 0.5236 to 0.5212, now 0.90 percent better than naive, still short of the margin. For Chronos-2 they are worse in all 6 matched configs. Holiday dummies did not help Greykite, and Silverkite's trend and seasonality terms drift badly past two weeks.

Every model subclasses AbstractModelWrapper (train, predict, save, load) and takes a config class that subclasses AbstractConfigWrapper (defaults, validation, grid, search space, and what the backtester needs). The backtester, optimizers, and publisher work with any of them.

NaiveModel. What it does: Repeats the last price. The baseline every other model has to beat. GradientBoostingModel. What it does: scikit-learn gradient boosted trees on recent daily price changes, plus optional degree days and calendar features. Forecasts several days ahead by feeding each prediction back in. GreykiteModel. What it does: LinkedIn Greykite Silverkite: trend, seasonality, recent prices as lags, and US holiday dummies as regressors. Each holiday gets a dummy for the day itself and for up to 4 days before and after (labor_day_pre_2, labor_day_post_1). Dummies that are never 1 in the training window are left out.

ChronosModel. What it does: Amazon Chronos-2, a pretrained time series model, used zero-shot on CPU. Degree days and calendar features can be passed as known future covariates. Tuned on context length, weather, and the yearly terms.

section: How it works > Data, backtests, search, and publishing
text: ForecastDataProvider. Job: Give it an as-of date and it returns a ForecastWindow: training data on or before that date, feature values for the dates to predict, and the actual prices used to score the forecast.

section: How it works > Data, backtests, search, and publishing
text: AbstractFeatureSource. Job: Base class for extra data. Each source returns only what was known on the as-of date. WeatherFeatureSource adds heating and cooling degree days. HolidayFeatureSource adds US holiday dummies from the holidays package, which are known in advance and so are valid for the forecast dates. CalendarFeatureSource adds Fourier terms for the time of year (2 harmonics) and day of week (1 or 2 harmonics) and an after_weekend flag for the first weekday after a weekend; these depend only on the date. Only the yearly terms are tuned. StorageFeatureSource adds the EIA storage level once each weekly report is published.

section: How it works > Data, backtests, search, and publishing
text: Backtester. Job: For each as-of date gets the window, checks for leakage, trains a fresh model, predicts, and records a BacktestResult. Runs dates in parallel with n_jobs. BacktestReport, ForecastMetrics. Job: Score one config: MAE, RMSE, MAPE, WAPE, and bias, overall, by days ahead, and by horizon bucket (days 1 to 5, 6 to 15, 16 to 30). AbstractOptimizer. Job: Backtests candidate configs, logs each one as a nested MLflow run, skips repeats, records failures without stopping, and builds the results table with skill against naive.

section: How it works > Data, backtests, search, and publishing
text: GridSearchOptimizer, BayesianOptimizer. Job: Every combination in the grid, or Optuna's TPE sampler picking each next config from the ones already scored. ModelPublisher. Job: Publishes the best config only if it lowers error by at least min_improvement against naive (1 percent by default). The chosen config is retrained on all data, logged as an MLflow pyfunc model, registered, and given the champion alias. TuningPipeline. Job: Runs all of the above from tuning.yaml. natgas tune calls it.

section: How it works > Data, backtests, search, and publishing
text: To add a model, create a folder under models/ with a config class and a model class, add the pair to ModelCatalog, and give it a grid and search space in tuning.yaml. Nothing else changes.

Training data always ends on the as-of date, and the test period starts the next trading day. The backtester checks this on every window. Storage values only appear once EIA would have published them (6 days after the week ends).

Weather for future dates would come from the forecast made on the as-of date. Past forecasts are not stored, so backtests use the observed weather as a perfect forecast. This makes weather models look better than they will live, and much more so at 30 days than at 5: real weather forecasts lose most of their skill after about two weeks, while the backtest still hands the models the exact weather for days 16 to 30. Pass use_observed_as_forecast=False to WeatherFeatureSource to hide future weather instead. Production scoring cannot see future weather either, so it uses the real forecast and then normals (see below).

No single model wins every horizon. In the backtests gradient boosting is best over days 6 to 15, Chronos-2 is best over days 16 to 30, and over days 1 to 5 nothing clearly beats repeating the last price. So instead of crowning one model, the daily job runs a tournament, organized like the Olympics.

Trials. Every model family (Chronos-2, gradient boosting, Greykite) has its own MLflow registered model, natgas-chronos, natgas-gradient-boosting, and natgas-greykite, each with a @champion and a @challenger. A challenger is a model in trials. It is scored every day next to its family champion, and it earns the title only after 60 matured production days with a lower blended MAE than the champion. When that happens the aliases swap: the challenger becomes @champion, and the former champion goes back to trials as @challenger, also tagged @legacy_champion. Naive is not a family. It is the baseline, natgas-naive@baseline, scored every day so everyone has something to beat.

Events. Family champions compete in three events, one per horizon: days 1 to 5, days 6 to 15, and days 16 to 30. To qualify for an event a champion must follow the domain rules and beat naive in that event by at least min_improvement (1 percent lower error). The qualified champion with the lowest blended MAE wins the event. If nobody qualifies, naive wins it, because a model that does not clearly beat "repeat the last price" is not worth the risk. The scorecard. Trials and events use the same blended score. A model is judged on the last 30 as-of dates whose forecasts have matured in production. A new model has little production history, so its backtest fills the rest of the window:

On day one the score is the backtest MAE of that exact version in that exact bucket. After 15 matured days it is half production and half backtest. After 30 it is pure production. If a version has no backtest score for a bucket, the naive backtest MAE stands in. The podium. The three event winners are stitched into one 30 day forecast, saved as stage production in predictions. That is the business facing forecast for the dashboard. Each row keeps the model and registry version of the winner that produced it, and the numbers are copies of what that winner forecast in its own stage, so what is published is exactly what was scored.

Domain rules. Chronos-2 must use weather covariates, and Greykite must not use weather. Seeding only picks configs that follow them, the scorer refuses to score a config that breaks them, and a rule breaker cannot qualify for an event. Opening day, as of 2026-11-18. Every contender has zero matured production days, so every blended MAE is its backtest MAE:

Days 1 to 5. Winner: Naive (natgas-naive v1). Blended MAE: 0.2476. Naive: 0.2476. Better than naive: 0.00%. Also ran: gradient boosting 0.2473 (0.15%, short of the 1% margin), Chronos-2 0.2518, Greykite 0.3039. Days 6 to 15. Winner: Gradient boosting (natgas-gradient-boosting v1). Blended MAE: 0.4594. Naive: 0.4656. Better than naive: 1.34%. Also ran: Chronos-2 0.4628 (0.61%), Greykite 0.6123.

Days 16 to 30. Winner: Chronos-2 (natgas-chronos v1). Blended MAE: 0.6459. Naive: 0.6589. Better than naive: 1.98%. Also ran: gradient boosting 0.6537 (0.79%), Greykite 0.9629. The published forecast for 2026-11-18 is naive for days 1 to 5, gradient boosting for days 6 to 15, and Chronos-2 with its 80 percent interval for days 16 to 30. Chronos-2 without weather scored 0.5204 in the grid, second best, but it breaks the weather rule, so the next best weather config is the challenger. Greykite's second best config (holiday window 2 with holidays off) forecasts exactly the same as the best one, so the seeder skips it and takes the next distinct config.

section: The model tournament > Replaying the past as production
text: A new tournament has no production record, so the scorecard leans on backtests for its first 30 days and no trial can finish for 60. natgas tournament simulate builds that record by replaying past trading days as if each one were today. For every day, oldest first, prices, weather, and storage after that day are dropped before any model sees them. There is no stored weather forecast from back then, so every future date gets the 10 year smoothed daily normal from weather observed up to that day. Every contender is scored under a run id that starts with sim_, matured forecasts get their actual price, and the tournament runs for that day. Live runs after the replay get plain hex run ids, so the dashboard can tell the two apart.

section: The model tournament > Replaying the past as production
text: --trim-backtests keeps backtests and production apart: backtests made on or after the first replayed day are removed from backtest_forecasts and its Parquet copy, and each version's backtest_ tags are rescored from forecasts whose target date came before that day, so the scorecard never borrows a price the replay has not reached yet. --reset empties predictions, forecast_actuals, and the tournament tables first.

section: The model tournament > Replaying the past as production
text: natgas tournament seed refuses to run when a family already has a champion, so trial progress is never wiped by accident. It also widens the stage column of older databases (StageColumnMigrator) and relabels the pre-tournament rows, so production only ever means the tournament's published forecast.

natgas score (or make score) is the daily job. Run it by hand, from cron with scripts/run_scoring.sh, or as a Prefect flow (see Prefect below). DataRefresher reloads the last 30 days of prices, weather, and storage with the same loaders as natgas ingest, so late corrections replace earlier values.

The as-of date is the latest trading day before today. Today's bar is still trading, so it is never used. ProductionScorer loads every contender from its registry alias (@champion and @challenger of each family, and natgas-naive@baseline), refits each version's config on data through the as-of date, the same way every backtest ran, and saves 30 rows per contender under its own stage. The scorer refuses a Chronos-2 config without weather or a Greykite config with weather.

ActualsRefresher copies every forecast whose target date has a price into forecast_actuals, with the actual and the error, and ForecastMonitor recreates the forecast_accuracy and forecast_accuracy_rolling views: MAE, MAPE, WAPE, and bias by stage and horizon bucket (days 1 to 5, 6 to 15, 16 to 30, and all days), over all matured forecasts and over the last 20 as-of dates. ModelTournament judges the 60 day trials and promotes any challenger that earned it, scores every contender on the blended scorecard, runs the three events, saves the standings, winners, and trial progress, and stitches the winners into stage production.

PredictionStore only appends. A stage that already has rows for the as-of date is skipped, and the table key (as_of_date, stage, horizon_day) blocks duplicates, so reruns are safe. The tournament tables are keyed by as-of date, so a rerun replaces that day's standings instead of adding to them.

Future weather. Chronos-2 uses degree days for the 30 forecast days, and those days have not happened yet. ForecastWeatherFeatureSource fills them with the Open-Meteo forecast that the weather loader stores (14 days, weather.forecast_days in config/settings.yaml, which covers about 10 trading days) and, after that, the daily normal: the average degree days for that day of the year over the last 10 years, smoothed over 15 days. The backtests used observed weather for all 30 days, so expect live accuracy on days 11 to 30 to sit closer to Chronos-2 without weather. The blended scorecard picks that up on its own as production days replace backtest days. Forecast dates past the last price skip exchange holidays (TradingCalendar), so every forecast gets an actual.
Or open notebooks/run_daily_update.ipynb and run all cells to do the same job by hand.

Ingestion, backtesting, MLflow tracking, the family registries, the daily scoring job, and the tournament exist today. The dashboard is planned. The scoring job can run on a schedule with cron or Prefect.
